content: Filipin was first isolated in 1955 by chemists at the Upjohn Company. It was derived from the mycelium and culture filtrates of a previously unknown actinomycete, Streptomyces filipinensis, which had been discovered in a soil sample collected from the Philippine Islands. The compound was named Filipin in reference to its origin. This isolate demonstrated potent antifungal activity. Based on its characteristic UV-Vis and IR spectra, Filipin was identified as a polyene macrolide. Although polyene macrolide antibiotics exhibit strong antifungal properties, most of them are too toxic for therapeutic use. The notable exceptions to this are amphotericin B and nystatin A1. Unlike amphotericin B and nystatin A1, which form sterol-dependent ion channels, Filipin is believed to act as a simple membrane disruptor. Filipin is highly fluorescent and binds specifically to cholesterol, which has made it widely used as a histochemical stain for cholesterol. This method of detecting cholesterol in cell membranes is clinically applied in the study and diagnosis of Niemann-Pick disease Type C. Additionally, Filipin is used in cellular biology as an inhibitor of the raft/caveolae endocytosis pathway in mammalian cells, typically at concentrations around 3 µg/mL. Filipin is not a single compound but rather a mixture of four components, collectively referred to as the Filipin complex. These components are Filipin I (4%), Filipin II (25%), Filipin III (53%), and Filipin IV (18%). The major component, Filipin III, has a structure that was proposed by Ceder and Ryhage for the Filipin complex. Filipin I, which has been challenging to characterize, is likely a mixture of several components, each with two fewer hydroxyl groups than Filipin III. Mass spectrometry and NMR data suggest that Filipin II is 1'-deoxy-Filipin III. Filipin IV is isomeric to Filipin III, with their NMR spectra being nearly identical. The primary difference lies in the splitting pattern of the proton at the C2 position, indicating that Filipin IV is likely epimeric to Filipin III at either the C1' or C3 position. The relative and absolute stereochemistry of Filipin III was determined through 13C NMR acetonide analysis.
